_note: Fixed 'Earth cannot reproduce this' text per target body, shown on every card. Gravity, vacuum and the lunar night are never scored. Factors no Earth place can ever truly match but that still differ from place to place (oxygen, CO2, ozone, UV-C, cosmic-ray dose) are scored at a quarter weight (features.json "weight") and named here. Each line also says what a future base must provide, and where the matching test can be done instead.
moon: Gravity: the Moon pulls at about 1.6 m/s2, one sixth of Earth. No Earth site can reproduce it, so walking, digging and dust behaviour differ.
Vacuum: the Moon has almost no atmosphere. Earth's air changes heat flow, dust motion and how equipment cools.

Radiation: about 1.37 mSv a day from cosmic rays (Chang'e-4), roughly 1,600 times Ireland's and 70 times Earth's highest plateaus, plus solar storms with no shelter. Scored at a quarter weight because no Earth site can match it. A base needs regolith cover or a lava tube and a storm shelter; tests use particle accelerators, the ISS and Artemis, not an Earth analog.
Lunar night: dark and cold for about two weeks at a time everywhere except a few polar peaks. No Earth site matches that cycle.

Air and UV shield: none. Oxygen and ozone count only a quarter as much as other comparisons, because no Earth site can match a vacuum. A lunar base must make all its oxygen, for example from regolith (oxygen is about 45 percent of lunar rock by mass), and shield crews and plants from unfiltered UV.

UV: unfiltered sunlight with UV-C (up to about 2 W/m2 day-and-night average at the equator) and about 10 times Earth's strongest UV-B. UV-C is scored at a quarter weight (Earth has none); UV-B in full, so Earth's high, dry deserts score best. Suits, visors, windows and plastics need UV-rated materials; test them under UV lamps.
mars: Gravity: Mars pulls at about 3.7 m/s2, 38 percent of Earth. Earth cannot reproduce it outside a short parabolic flight.
Thin atmosphere: Mars surface pressure is under one percent of Earth's and almost all carbon dioxide, so wind, dust and heat transfer behave differently.

Radiation: about 0.6 to 0.8 mSv a day at the ground (Curiosity RAD), roughly 30 to 40 times Earth's highest plateaus (and over 100 times most places); lower in deep basins, higher on the volcanoes. Scored at a quarter weight because no Earth site can match it. A base needs regolith cover and a storm shelter; tests use particle accelerators, the ISS and Artemis.
Soil chemistry: Martian soil carries perchlorates that most Earth analog soils lack.

Air and UV shield: the air is 95 percent CO2 with about 1 Pa of oxygen and almost no ozone. Oxygen, CO2 and ozone count only a quarter as much as other comparisons, because no Earth site can match them. A Mars base must make its oxygen from that CO2 (Perseverance's MOXIE made 122 g in 2021 to 2023) and block UV in suits, windows and greenhouses.

UV: Mars gets UV-C (about 0.4 to 0.6 W/m2 on average) that Earth's ozone removes, and 2 to 3 times the UV-B of Earth's strongest places (Atacama, Altiplano, Tibet). UV-C is scored at a quarter weight; UV-B in full. UV also sterilises the surface: good for planetary protection, bad for exposed materials and any greenhouse.
